Title: Distinguish numerical variables
Learning intention: I am learning to identify discrete and continuous numerical data
Teaching support: Counts are discrete; measurements can take values between whole numbers.
Worked example: A class records the number of cars in a car park for 25 students. Is this variable discrete or continuous? Type discrete or continuous. Given: See the question text. Answer: Discrete. It is a count, so it changes in whole steps.
Reasoning example: Leo weighed bags to the nearest kilogram and says mass is discrete. What type of variable is it? Type discrete or continuous. Given: See the question text. Answer: Continuous. Mass is measured, not counted. Rounding hides values between whole kilograms.
Application example: A survey records four variables: height of a seedling; number of texts sent in a day; time taken to run 100 m; daily rainfall. How many of these variables are continuous? Worked example: Two fertilisers are compared on seedlings. Which method is fairer? Given: See the question text. Answer: Give both groups the same water, light and pot size, and measure every seedling. Keep everything except the thing being tested the same, and collect repeated observations.
Reasoning example: Design A was flown 10 times and Design B only twice. What limits the conclusion? Given: See the question text. Answer: Two flights may not show how Design B usually performs. A fair comparison changes only one thing and collects enough observations of each design.
Application example: On average, how much further did Design B fly than Design A? Given: Flight distances under the same conditions (m). Design; Distances: A, 7, 4, 5, 8, 7, 5; B, 9, 11, 8, 11, 7, 8. Answer: 3. Mean A = 36 ÷ 6 = 6. Mean B = 54 ÷ 6 = 9. Difference = 3 m.

Title: Check unusual measurements
Learning intention: I am learning to decide how to handle an unusual observation
Teaching support: Check units, recording and measurement before deciding what to do.
Worked example: A reaction time of 0 seconds appears in the data. What should the investigator do? Given: See the question text. Answer: Check the recording, because a reaction time cannot be 0 seconds. An unusual value may be a real observation or an error. Check it before deciding what to do.
Reasoning example: One height was recorded in metres by mistake. Type that value in centimetres. Given: Student heights (cm): 155, 136, 1.46, 164, 157, 160. Answer: 146. 1.46 m × 100 = 146 cm.
Application example: One height was recorded in metres by mistake. After correcting it, what is the mean height? Given: Student heights (cm): 155, 136, 1.46, 164, 157, 160. Answer: 153. Correct 1.46 m to 146 cm. Total = 918, so the mean is 918 ÷ 6 = 153.

Title: Evaluate a design improvement
Learning intention: I am learning to use distributions to evaluate a practical claim
Teaching support: Compare typical performance and variation under matched conditions.
Worked example: Type the mean distance for each design. Given: Distances under matched conditions (cm). Design; Distances: A, 41, 30, 47, 46, 36; B, 35, 39, 54, 41, 46. Answer: 40, 43. A: 200 ÷ 5 = 40. B: 215 ÷ 5 = 43.
Reasoning example: Which statement fairly describes these results? Given: Distances under matched conditions (cm). Design; Distances: A, 41, 30, 47, 46, 36; B, 35, 39, 54, 41, 46. Answer: B’s mean is 3 cm greater than A’s, and B’s range is larger. Means: A 40, B 43. Ranges: A 17, B 19. Describe what was recorded without claiming certainty about every future trial.

Title: Analyse continuous measurements
Learning intention: I am learning to summarise measured data with units
Teaching support: Calculate a suitable centre and range, then describe the distribution.
Worked example: What is the mean growth? Given: Growth of bean plants in one week (cm): 5.3, 4.1, 1.6, 2.9, 5.3. Answer: 3.84. Total = 19.2 cm. Mean = 19.2 ÷ 5 = 3.84 cm.
Reasoning example: Type the median and the range. Given: Growth of bean plants in one week (cm): 5.3, 4.1, 1.6, 2.9, 5.3. Answer: 4.1, 3.7. Ordered: 1.6, 2.9, 4.1, 5.3, 5.3. Median = 4.1. Range = 5.3 − 1.6 = 3.7.
Application example: How much greater is the mean growth with fertiliser? Given: Growth in one week (cm). Group; Growth: No fertiliser, 3.6, 2.9, 1.6, 2.3, 3.6; With fertiliser, 4.7, 2.9, 2.7, 2.9, 2.6. Answer: 0.36. Means: 2.8 cm and 3.16 cm. Difference = 0.36 cm.

Title: Support a conclusion
Learning intention: I am learning to report a claim supported by the data
Teaching support: State the comparison, numerical evidence and a relevant limitation.
Worked example: What do these results show? Given: Reaction time investigation. Group; Median (s); Range (s): A, 0.29, 0.08; B, 0.33, 0.05. Answer: A has the lower median time, and B has the smaller range. A lower median time means faster typical reactions; a smaller range means less spread between the extremes.
Reasoning example: A report claims Group B reacts faster than Group A. Which evidence best supports the claim? Given: See the question text. Answer: Group B’s median time is 0.06 s lower than Group A’s. A claim about typical performance needs a comparison of a centre, such as the median, not one person or the group size.
Application example: The adults’ median reaction time was 0.36 s. How many seconds lower is the teenagers’ median? Given: Teenagers’ reaction times (s): 0.32, 0.27, 0.18, 0.23, 0.32. Answer: 0.09. Teenagers’ median = 0.27 s. Difference = 0.36 − 0.27 = 0.09 s.

Title: Recognise investigation limits
Learning intention: I am learning to limit a conclusion to what the investigation supports
Teaching support: Explain which people, objects or conditions the collected data represent.
Worked example: A small group was measured once at the start of the day. What should the report point out? Given: See the question text. Answer: Other groups or times of day may give different results. Keep the conclusion within the people, conditions and evidence actually studied.
Reasoning example: An investigation into how far students in the school travel to school measured one class. Which change would let the conclusion apply more widely? Given: See the question text. Answer: Survey a random sample of students from every year level. A random sample from the whole group of interest is more likely to represent it than a convenient group.
Application example: A survey asked 180 students at a school of 1200 students. What percentage of the school was surveyed? Given: See the question text. Answer: 15. 180 ÷ 1200 × 100 = 15%. The rest of the school was not surveyed, so the report should say so.
